You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Arjun

Arjun was twenty when his older cousin Rohan died. It was a Tuesday in March, unremarkable except for the phone call from his mother, her voice fractured in a way he had never heard before. Rohan had been driving home from work—a software engineer, stable, careful, the kind of person everyone said had his life figured out. A drunk driver crossed the median on the interstate. Rohan was pronounced dead at the scene. There had been no warning, no illness, no time to say anything. One moment he existed; the next, he didn't. For Arjun, who had grown up in the same house as Rohan during his childhood, who had watched him navigate college and career with a steadiness Arjun secretly envied, the event shattered something fundamental about how he understood safety. The world, he had come to believe, was a place where ordinary Tuesday mornings could end in death. Randomness was the only rule.

In the weeks after the funeral, Arjun tried to write. He had been working on a novel—a small literary project he had been quietly proud of—but the words felt hollow now, contaminated by the knowledge that none of it mattered if everything could be taken away without reason. He abandoned the manuscript. More pressingly, when his parents began asking him about college applications, about whether he would apply for jobs, about what came next, Arjun found himself unable to answer. The future felt like a trap. If he made plans, if he allowed himself to imagine anything—a career, a relationship, a life—he was only setting himself up for devastation. So he stopped planning. He refused to discuss it. His mother would ask if he had looked at internships; he would change the subject or leave the room. The avoidance felt necessary, protective. Not planning meant nothing could be taken from him.

Yet the avoidance created its own torment. Without plans, without forward motion, Arjun felt unmoored, and that formlessness fed a deepening conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that he was powerless within it. His inability to imagine a future began to feel like evidence that no future was worth imagining—that nothing he did mattered, that safety was an illusion. He became hypervigilant in ways he did not fully recognize. Sounds made him jump: a car horn outside his window would send adrenaline flooding through his chest. He could not relax even when sitting alone in his bedroom with the door locked. His body seemed to expect catastrophe at every moment. Sleep became nearly impossible. He would lie awake for hours, his mind cycling through scenarios—car crashes, sudden illnesses, the random violence that had taken Rohan. When he did sleep, he woke gasping.

The avoidance of grief reminders became another layer of the trap. Anything connected to Rohan—a song that had played at the funeral, the software company's logo glimpsed in an advertisement, even the sight of someone driving a silver sedan like Rohan's—triggered a wave of panic and despair. So Arjun began to avoid more and more. He stopped going to the coffee shop where he used to write because Rohan had taken him there once. He declined invitations to family gatherings where relatives might mention Rohan's name. He isolated himself, telling himself this was the only way to manage the grief, but what actually happened was that his world grew smaller and his conviction that he was fundamentally unsafe grew larger.

By late summer, five months after Rohan's death, Arjun was stuck in a cycle he could not name. The more he avoided—the future, reminders, social situations—the more his belief that the world was dangerous and that he was helpless intensified. And the more convinced he became of that danger, the more he needed to avoid, to seek reassurance from his parents that he was okay, that nothing bad would happen to him. He would call his mother at work and ask her to confirm he was safe, and for a few minutes after she reassured him, the panic would subside. But it always returned, sharper each time. His parents, alarmed by his deterioration, finally insisted he see someone. Arjun came to the first appointment exhausted and terrified, unable to articulate why he felt so broken, only knowing that he had lost not just his cousin but his ability to believe in tomorrow.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: While the vignette describes negative appraisals (the world is dangerous, randomness is the only rule, the future is a trap, safety is an illusion) and maladaptive strategies (avoidance of planning, avoidance of reminders, isolation), no paragraph explicitly conveys that the appraisals drive or lead to the avoidance behaviors. The causal direction is unclear or implicit rather than explicitly stated.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: Although maladaptive strategies (avoidance) and threat perception (hypervigilance, panic, sense of danger) both appear, the vignette does not clearly establish that the avoidance behaviors themselves intensify the sense of threat. The cycle is described ("the more he avoided... the more his belief that the world was dangerous... intensified"), but this relationship is stated only in the final paragraph in a general summary form and lacks explicit causal language connecting the avoidance to increased threat perception within a coherent explanatory frame.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The world, he had come to believe, was a place where ordinary Tuesday mornings could end in death. Randomness was the only rule.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
If the world operated by pure chance and safety was an illusion, then planning for a future was an act of denial—a way of pretending he had control when he had none. So when his parents asked about internships and applications, Arjun's refusal was not mere avoidance; it was the logical consequence of a worldview in which the future could not be trusted and forward motion was foolish.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Yet the avoidance created its own torment. Without plans, without forward motion, Arjun felt unmoored, and that formlessness fed a deepening conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that he was powerless within it.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But more insidiously, the avoidance itself became evidence. By refusing to plan, by staying home, by not testing whether the world was actually as catastrophic as his mind insisted, Arjun's nervous system never received the counter-evidence it needed. Each day he stayed isolated, each moment he did not venture out, his body interpreted as confirmation that the threat was real and ongoing—that his fear, however overwhelming, was justified.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
By late summer, five months after Rohan's death, Arjun was stuck in a cycle he could not name. The more he avoided—the future, reminders, social situations—the more his belief that the world was dangerous and that he was helpless intensified.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The avoidance had become its own trap: by never staying in a situation long enough to discover it was safe, by never allowing his body to calm in the presence of what frightened him, he ensured that his sense of threat remained as sharp as the day Rohan died.
<<<END>>>
